opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, going into Llama 2 I was a bit of a skeptic. I came from a supervised learning background, and my intuition was that if you want a model to write well, you just collect really high-quality demonstrations and fine-tune on them. RLHF felt like an expensive, finicky detour.

What changed my mind was seeing where human annotators are actually good and where they're not. When you ask someone to *write* the ideal answer, you're capped by that person's ability. Most annotators can't write a perfect poem or a flawless piece of code on demand. But almost anyone can look at two outputs and tell you which one is better. Comparing is much easier than generating. That asymmetry turned out to be the key.

So with supervised fine-tuning, the model imitates the distribution of human writing, including all its flaws. With preference data and RL, the model explores, produces things, and gets told "this one's better than that one." Over iterations it can climb above the level of any individual annotator, because the signal is relative, not an absolute ceiling. We saw that concretely: after a few rounds of RLHF, the model's outputs were often preferred over the human-written SFT annotations themselves. At that point it didn't make much sense to keep paying people to write answers. It made more sense to have them judge the model's answers.

The other thing I underestimated was the iterative part. Each round, the model gets better, so the distribution of outputs shifts, so you need fresh preference data on the new distribution, and the reward model has to keep up. It's less a single training step and more a loop between humans and the model, and that loop is really where the magic is.

So my short answer: RLHF works not because RL is magical, but because it lets you use human judgment, which scales better than human demonstration, and it lets the model go beyond the humans supervising it.

r001.rationale: The response says that after a few rounds of RLHF, model outputs were often preferred over the human-written SFT annotations.

r002.rationale: It says supervised fine-tuning makes the model imitate human writing, “including all its flaws.”

r003.rationale: It contrasts the difficulty of writing an ideal answer with how much easier it is to compare answers, even when the judge could not produce a perfect answer themselves.

r004.rationale: The response describes comparative feedback and says the model can improve, but it does not clearly explain that preference training shifts probability away from poorer answers and toward better ones.

r005.rationale: It explicitly says the model can climb above any individual annotator and go beyond the humans supervising it.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think when we started Llama 2, honestly, a lot of us on the team were skeptical of RLHF. I came from NLP, from academia, and the conventional wisdom there was that RL is unstable, it's hard to make work, and supervised fine-tuning on good human demonstrations should be enough. If you have enough high-quality annotated data, you just imitate it. That was my prior.

And what changed my mind was actually a very simple observation while we were collecting data. We had these annotators writing responses, very good annotators, and at some point we looked at the outputs of the model after RLHF and compared them to what the annotators were writing. And the model's outputs were better. The annotators themselves preferred them. That was a bit of a shock, because the model was supposedly learning from these people, so how could it exceed them?

The way I understand it now is that there's a fundamental asymmetry between generating and judging. If I ask you to write a poem, and I ask you to compare two poems and say which one is better, the second task is much easier. Humans are much more reliable as judges than as writers. So with SFT, you're bottlenecked by the quality of what humans can produce. With RLHF, you're bottlenecked by what humans can distinguish, and that ceiling is much higher. You're essentially using the reward model to extract a signal that the annotators couldn't have written down directly, but that they can recognize.

The other thing is the distribution question. In SFT, you're forcing the model to put probability mass on one specific response, one specific wording, when there are many equally valid ones. That's a very noisy signal. With RLHF, you sample from the model's own distribution and you just push it toward the better samples. So you're learning in the model's own space, in its own words, rather than imposing a human's phrasing on it. I think that matters more than people realize for things like style and consistency.

And then there's the practical side. We found that this process is iterative. We did multiple rounds, RLHF v1 through v5, and each time we collected preferences on outputs from the latest model, retrained the reward model, and went again. The reward model has to keep up with the policy, otherwise it gets exploited. So RLHF isn't one technique, it's really a data flywheel. That was the big lesson: the scaling that matters is not just compute, it's human feedback on the current model's distribution, over and over.

So I went in thinking it was a nice-to-have on top of SFT, and I came out thinking it's the thing. SFT is mostly there to get you to a starting point where the samples are good enough to compare. The real alignment, and honestly a lot of the capability on open-ended tasks, comes from the RL.

r001.rationale: The response says that after RLHF, model outputs were better than the annotators’ written responses, and that the annotators preferred them.

r002.rationale: It does not say that imitating human answers also teaches the model to reproduce human mistakes.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says humans are more reliable at judging which answer is better than at writing answers themselves.

r004.rationale: It says RLHF samples from the model’s distribution and pushes it toward better samples, communicating a shift toward better outputs and away from poorer ones.

r005.rationale: It reports that the RLHF model’s outputs were better than the annotators’ own writing, showing performance beyond their ability to create answers.

astra-6.text:
What surprised me was how much of the capability was already there. Before working on Llama 2, I thought of RLHF more as teaching the model something new. But a lot of what we saw looked like learning to select the right behavior from things the model could already do.

Pretraining teaches you to predict text, and text contains everything: good answers, bad answers, people being helpful, people being unhelpful. That objective doesn’t tell you which behavior a user actually wants. Human feedback gives you a signal for that.

And there’s an important difference between showing the model one good answer and letting it generate answers and then comparing them. With supervised fine-tuning, you say, “Imitate this.” With reinforcement learning, you can say, “Of these possibilities, this one is better.” That gives you a way to improve behavior even when there isn’t one uniquely correct response.

So my understanding shifted toward RLHF as a way of making existing capabilities accessible and reliable. Of course, you’re optimizing a proxy for human preferences, so whether the reward actually reflects what you want remains a central problem.

r001.rationale: The response does not report that model-generated answers were usually judged better than human-written supervised fine-tuning answers.

r002.rationale: It says pretraining includes helpful and unhelpful text, but does not explain that cloning human answers also reproduces human mistakes.

r003.rationale: It does not state that humans can judge answer quality beyond their own ability to produce answers.

r004.rationale: It describes choosing better behavior among possibilities, but does not explain that preference training shifts the output distribution from poorer answers toward better ones.

r005.rationale: It does not state that RLHF can produce models that outperform annotators’ ability to create answers.

sol-6.1.text:
Training Llama 2 changed my intuition about what RLHF is doing. A common view was that pretraining gives the model its capabilities, and then alignment is mostly about making it polite or teaching it to follow a particular format. But we saw that the reinforcement learning stage could make a substantial difference to the quality of its answers.

The way I think about it is that the pretrained model already knows many possible ways to respond, including very good ones and very bad ones. Predicting the next token doesn’t necessarily favor the response you would want an assistant to give. Human feedback gives you a signal about which of those behaviors to reinforce.

And that creates an interesting asymmetry: it can be easier to recognize a good answer than to write one. With supervised fine-tuning, you’re asking people to produce demonstrations. With preferences, they can compare answers, and the model can learn from that judgment. So RLHF isn’t simply adding knowledge. It’s helping the model use what it has learned in a way that better matches what people actually want.

r001.rationale: It says RLHF improved answer quality but does not report that model-generated answers were usually judged better than human-written SFT answers.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that copying human demonstrations also reproduces human mistakes.

r003.rationale: It says recognizing a good answer can be easier than writing one, and that people can compare answers and provide judgments.

r004.rationale: It describes the pretrained model as having good and bad response behaviors and says feedback reinforces the preferred behaviors, conveying a shift toward better answers and away from poorer ones.

r005.rationale: It says humans may find judging easier than writing, but does not state that RLHF models can outperform annotators’ ability to create answers.
